I would like to share my experience regarding the handling of my cat during her spaying.

When I came to pick her up, my cat was still under the effects of the anesthesia and was extremely disoriented and terrified. She refused to go into her carrier. The assistant then grabbed her with a blanket and forced all four of her legs into the small crate.
This scene deeply shocked me. I completely understand that an animal can be difficult to handle, but I would have expected a much gentler and more reassuring approach, especially with an animal still under the effects of anesthesia and already very panicked.
What worries me most is that this experience seems to have left a real mark on my cat. Since this incident, she reacts strongly to hands and remains wary when anyone tries to handle her. Even now, several weeks later, I can see that she seems traumatized by this experience.

I also regret that there was no proper check-in with me upon discharge, nor sufficiently detailed explanations regarding post-operative care and monitoring of the incision.

I do not question the necessity of sterilization, but I believe that the way an animal is handled, particularly when vulnerable and under anesthesia, is just as important as the procedure itself.
I share this opinion so that, in my view, the management of stress and fear in animals can be given greater consideration.
Very helpful and always available team.

This clinic helped save my cat Berlioz not once, but twice. And the second time was nothing short of a miracle. Eternal gratitude.

I would not recommend this practice, and I would like to share my experience.

After my dog ​​broke a claw, he underwent two surgeries at €200 each. The post-operative instructions were vague, and basically, I was told to "remove the bandage in 10 days and it will be better."
During the first surgery, part of the claw was left in place. I don't know if this was intentional, but it resulted in an infection 10 days later, necessitating a second surgery to remove "the remaining part of the claw that was causing the problem." One surgery should have been sufficient.
Despite my repeated requests, no antibiotics were prescribed during the second surgery. The result: another infection, a swollen toe (which is now deformed).

Fearing I would have to pay another €200 for an unsatisfactory result, I consulted another veterinarian, who was visibly surprised by the condition of the paw and the lack of treatment.

In the end, it cost €400 plus about €100 at the new vet, for a procedure that didn't seem particularly complex to me. I'm now struggling to find the right word to describe this experience. And frankly, the claw still hasn't healed properly.

The doctor was actually quite available when I first explained my problem. This ultimately left me with the impression of being rushed and negligent. Perhaps other factors were at play, maybe I went to the clinic at a bad time, or there are circumstances I'm unaware of.

But in the end, I regret going there for my dog's treatment.

My cat recently fell ill, so I went to this clinic and was able to get an appointment very quickly. The vet is incredibly kind to animals, and most importantly, he took the time to explain in detail the illness my cat had and the reason behind each symptom.

He also took the time to explain the results of the tests he had performed and the function of each medication.
It might seem obvious, but I've rarely encountered such professional and reassuring veterinarians.
It's truly heartwarming to see that qualified people love their work and that you can trust them completely.
My cat is doing much better now, and I wouldn't hesitate to go back.
Thank you to the whole team for being so caring with my pet and me. 👏

A medical error resulting in poisoning nearly cost my 9-month-old puppy his life. The clinic sold me a dewormer that is absolutely forbidden for dogs of breeds susceptible to carrying a mutated MDR1 gene. A test exists to determine if a dog has the mutated gene, but the owner cannot possibly know that this condition exists, let alone that a test is available, if the veterinarian treating the animal has never mentioned it. This veterinarian, who has been treating Victor since he was two months old and therefore knows him well, NEVER mentioned it to me. Victor suffered seizures, excessive salivation, loss of balance, and a life-threatening prognosis upon arrival at the emergency room, even though he had been running around that very morning. The responsible veterinarian didn't even bother to contact me afterward to explain or apologize; he simply informed me through his assistants that his insurance company would contact me regarding reimbursement for the hospitalization costs. The decision was later confirmed by phone by the regional group manager, who called me from a blocked number (so clever to avoid being contacted again by a disgruntled customer!) to offer a rehearsed apology, this time on behalf of the group, in such a dehumanizing manner. My only advice: run far, far away.

Today, Victor is just over two years old. He hasn't grown a single centimeter since his hospitalization and still looks like a 9-month-old puppy. His new veterinarian attributes this stunted growth to the trauma caused by this "accident." Victor has also become reactive to humans and suffers from acute anxiety (since his return from the hospital). The nutritional supplements I give him to calm him will obviously never be covered by the clinic responsible for this distress: the Argos Lyon Monplaisir Veterinary Clinic.
